questions.question: What is the codomain of a function?
options: The set of inputs of the function.
The set where all outputs must lie.
Only the outputs actually attained by the function.
A rule for differentiating the function.
questions.explanation: For a specified map $f\colon X\to Y$, the codomain is the declared target set $Y$ in which every output must lie.
questions.source_support: Definition of codomain.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The input set is the domain $X$, not the codomain $Y$.
The outputs actually attained form the range, which may be a proper subset of the codomain.
A differentiation rule is an operation on functions, not a set of permitted outputs.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: How is the range of a function related to its codomain?
options: The range is always a subset of the codomain.
The codomain is always a subset of the range.
The range and codomain are always disjoint.
The range is the same as the domain.
questions.explanation: Every actual value $f(x)$ must lie in the declared target $Y$, so $f(X)\subseteq Y$.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: range is always a subset of codomain.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted
option_explanations: This reverses containment; unused target values can lie in the codomain but outside the range.
The range lies inside the codomain and therefore cannot be disjoint unless the range is empty.
Domain and range contain inputs and attained outputs respectively and need not coincide.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why does the codomain matter for surjectivity?
options: Surjectivity depends only on the formula used for $f(x)$.
Surjectivity ignores target values not actually hit.
Surjectivity depends on whether the range fills the chosen codomain.
Surjectivity is checked only on the domain.
questions.explanation: A function is surjective exactly when for every chosen target $y\in Y$ there is an input with $f(x)=y$, equivalently when its range equals $Y$.
questions.source_support: Interpretation and relevant result mention that the codomain provides context for surjectivity and changing it can affect surjectivity.

The domain supplies candidate inputs, but surjectivity asks whether all codomain values are hit.

questions.question: Can changing only the codomain of a function produce a different function?
options: Changing the codomain never affects the function.
Changing the codomain can define a different function.
Changing the codomain changes the formula but not the target set.
Changing the codomain makes the domain empty.
questions.explanation: A function includes its domain, codomain, and assignment; changing the declared codomain changes that specification even if the formula is unchanged.
questions.skill_detail: codomain is part of a function
questions.source_support: A function is defined by its domain, codomain, and rule.

Changing only the codomain changes the target set, not the algebraic rule.
The domain remains whatever was declared; changing the target does not erase its inputs.

questions.question: Which distinction is important for the codomain concept?
options: The codomain is always exactly the range.
The codomain is the set of inputs.
The range is chosen before the function is evaluated.
Codomain is chosen with the function; range is the actual outputs.
